name: Habakkuk

objectives.text: Identify Habakkuk as a prophet who brought his questions to God in prayer
Retell how Habakkuk stood at his watchpost to wait for God's answer
Recite the words of Habakkuk 2:4 that the righteous shall live by his faith
Describe what Habakkuk said he would do even if the fig tree, vines, fields, and flocks all failed
Summarize Habakkuk's first complaint about violence and injustice going unpunished in Judah
Explain God's first answer that he was raising up the Chaldeans to bring judgment on Judah
Summarize Habakkuk's second complaint asking how a holy God could use a nation more wicked than Judah
Explain God's command to write the vision plainly and wait for it because it will surely come at the appointed time
Compare Habakkuk's honest questions addressed to God with Israel's grumbling against God in the wilderness
Identify how Habakkuk's prayer recalls God's past saving acts such as the Exodus and asks him in wrath to remember mercy
Outline the book of Habakkuk as a dialogue with God, a series of woes, and a closing prayer-psalm
Analyze how the dialogue between the prophet and God moves Habakkuk from complaint to confident trust
Explain how Habakkuk 3:17-19 grounds praise in God's character and salvation rather than in outward circumstances
Situate Habakkuk in the late seventh century BC as Babylon rose to power before invading Judah
Interpret Habakkuk 2:4 in context by contrasting the puffed-up soul of the proud with the righteous who live by faith
Explain the five woe oracles against the Chaldeans and identify the sin each one condemns
Explain how the promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord's glory and the call for silence before him frame the woes
Explain the Reformed doctrine of providence as Habakkuk shows God ordaining Babylon's rise while holding Babylon guilty for its sin
Construct a biblical response to the problem of evil drawing on God's answers to Habakkuk
Evaluate objections to God's sovereignty in using wicked nations by testing them against Habakkuk and related texts
Evaluate how Paul and Hebrews use Habakkuk 2:4 to teach justification by faith and persevering faith
Compose a prayer modeled on Habakkuk's pattern of honest lament, remembrance of God's works, and declared trust

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies: the two complaints, God's answers, the woe oracles, the dialogue analysis, Habakkuk 2:4 in context and in Paul, the historical setting, God's sovereignty, and the problem of evil. Turned the watchtower item into a retelling of Habakkuk waiting for God's answer. Reframed the items about rejoicing and the closing reflection as describing the text and composing a prayer on Habakkuk's pattern, so no objective asks for a feeling. Added objectives on the command to write and wait for the vision, the outline of the book, the prayer-psalm's recall of the Exodus, the framing verses of the woes, and providence. Added verse-level references and the confession articles on providence and justification.
